title: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere
subtitle: Air combat enters an imagined future
summary: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere is Namco's PlayStation aerial combat game, first released in Japan on 27 May 1999. Fighter missions move into a futuristic world, giving the series a science-fiction setting beyond its earlier contemporary aircraft conflicts. body: Ace Combat 3: Electrosphere is Namco's PlayStation aerial combat game, first released in Japan on 27 May 1999. Fighter missions move into a futuristic world, giving the series a science-fiction setting beyond its earlier contemporary aircraft conflicts. Players still pursue enemy formations and complete objectives from the cockpit, but the Japanese release places those sorties within a branching story. Decisions and relationships affect the route through the campaign. The result gives the next mission a narrative consequence alongside the immediate task of surviving it and bringing down the designated targets.

The Japanese edition spans two discs and uses its story to connect the player's choices to different missions and outcomes. Characters and rival interests become part of deciding where the pilot goes next. The aircraft and landscapes support that future setting, while the basic action remains accessible air combat rather than a strict simulation. Takuya Iwasaki and Atsushi Shiozawa directed the project, with a writing contribution from Dai Satō. Its ambition lies in making a flight campaign a story with alternatives rather than a single unchanging list of operations.

Financial constraints led to a substantially reduced international version, released in Europe and North America in 2000. The branching Japanese story and much of its presentation were removed, changing how the same combat was experienced. This difference helps explain the game's uneven reception across regions. The Japanese edition has since attracted renewed attention for its narrative ambition and unusual place within Ace Combat. Its electronic score, by a team including Tetsukazu Nakanishi, Hiroshi Okubo and Go Shiina, further separates this imagined future from the series' more familiar military settings.
